chunks.content: The rise of patient-specific models for human placental biology The placenta is a crucial organ that connects the mother and fetus, playing a vital role in fetal survival and development [ ]. It mediates nutrient and gas exchange at the maternal-fetal interface, regulates immune responses, and produces hormones for maintaining pregnancy [ ]. The human placenta consists of three types of trophoblast cells. Cytotrophoblasts ( CTs , see Glossary) are the highly proliferative stem cell population that can give rise to further differentiated syncytiotrophoblasts (STs) and extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs) [ ]. Abnormal placental function can lead to significant obstetric complications, including recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) , preeclampsia (PE) , fetal growth restriction (FGR), and placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) [ ]. Placental research is essential for understanding the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of pregnancy-related complications. Although access to human placental tissue is crucial for studying placental development and function, its acquisition and use have been limited by technical and ethical challenges [ , ]. Given the limited availability of early-stage human placental tissue, various in vitro models have been developed to investigate placental development, function, and the maintenance of pregnancy ( ). By adapting the established derivation and culture protocols by Okae et al. [ ], patient-specific trophoblast stem cells (pTSCs) have been generated from various sources, including human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), somatic fibroblasts, CTs obtained after completed pregnancies, and more recently, chorionic villus tissue obtained via chorionic villus sampling (CVS) during ongoing pregnancies ( ). pTSCs can retain the genetic and epigenetic abnormalities of individual pregnancies. By capturing inter-individual genetic diversity, research using pTSCs offers powerful tools for understanding placental development and the pathogenesis of pregnancy-related complications. Although pTSCs are emerging as key models for studying placental development and disorders, their derivation methods have not yet been comprehensively reviewed. In this review, we underscore the importance of pTSCs, evaluate their derivation methods, and provide insights into their applications. The need for pTSCs Placental development and the onset of related disorders are often closely associated with genomic alterations, including gene mutations, chromosomal abnormalities, and changes in transcriptomic and epigenomic signatures [ , ]. Many placental disorders exhibit distinct manifestations influenced by genetic background, immune responses, and environmentally driven epigenetic variation [ – ]. An analysis of the transcriptomic landscape in monosomy X placentas highlights the impact of chromosomal abnormalities on early placental development, suggesting that attenuated cytokine-signaling pathways affect immune regulation [ ]. Placentas with large-scale aneuploidies or copy-number variations (CNVs) are more frequently associated with small-for-gestational-age infants compared to karyotypically normal placentas [ ]. Such complexity is challenging to capture or interrogate using the limited number of available bona fide hTSC lines, which do not fully reflect genetic diversity or the broader transcriptomic and epigenomic landscapes ( ). Relying on these restricted models may undermine their physiological and clinical relevance, as well as the fidelity required to elucidate pathogenesis, predict individual risk, and develop personalized therapeutic strategies. In contrast, patient-specific models can be derived through reprogramming or direct induction from an individual’s cells, reflecting the patient’s genetic and epigenetic backgrounds. While disease-specific models are often developed with a focus on a particular condition [ ], patient-specific stem cells can maintain inter-individual variation even among patients with the same disease. They serve as valuable research models for mechanistic dissection, risk stratification, and therapy development by generating personalized placental models [ , ]. These models offer a precise and reproducible system that allows for systematic analysis of disorder-associated alterations in trophoblast proliferation, differentiation, invasiveness, and immune regulation. Even in the presence of the same mutation, inter-individual genetic and epigenetic differences can lead to varying degrees of cellular dysfunction [ , ]. By leveraging pTSCs, inter-individual differences in susceptibility to placental disorders can be evaluated in vitro . Certain pTSC-based approaches also alleviate ethical concerns and enable longitudinal follow-up of clinical outcomes ( ) ( ). This positions pTSCs as key platforms for placental disease research, patient-specific risk assessment, and therapy. pTSC derivation pTSCs can be generated via : (1) trans-differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) reprogrammed from patient somatic cells; (2) direct reprogramming from fibroblasts by forced expression of transcription factors (TFs); (3) derivation from CTs after the completion of pregnancy; and (4) derivation from chorionic villi collected via CVS during early pregnancy ( ). pTSCs trans-differentiated from iPSCs (iPSC-derived pTSCs) Earlier attempts at pTSC derivation involved reprogramming somatic cells into iPSCs, followed by trans-differentiation into hTSCs. Dong et al. reported that when naïve human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) or renal epithelial cell-derived iPSCs are cultured in hTSC medium (TSCM), a homogeneous cell population closely resembling bona fide hTSCs is produced, exhibiting similar gross morphology, surface markers, and trophoblast-specific gene expression [ ]. However, this model did not fully recapitulate the developmental continuum from pre-implantation to post-implantation stages, as cells representing the initial trophoblast lineage, trophectoderm (TE) , were not detected during the conversion of iPSCs into pTSCs. iPSC-derived pTSCs (iPSC-TSCs) were transcriptionally most similar to the human post-implantation TE lineage at day 12, with low levels of CDX2 [ ], a TF that is markedly downregulated in CTs as the first trimester progresses [ ]. In parallel, Cinkornpumin et al. showed that naïve hPSCs can be converted to hTSCs [ ]. In addition, their findings indicated substantial differences in conversion efficiency, lineage fidelity, and differentiation capacity of the TSCs, depending on the PSC state and cell lines. Shortly after, Io et al. induced pTSCs that more closely resemble pre-implantation-stage TE from naïve hESCs and iPSCs using the ACE culture condition, which contains A83–01, CHIR99021, and epidermal growth factor (EGF) [ ]. This method established an in vitro model that faithfully recapitulates the complete trajectory of trophoblast development from pre- to post-implantation. The derived pTSCs have met established criteria for human first-trimester trophoblasts, including extended self-renewal, bipotency, lack of HLA class I expression, an active miRNA cluster on chromosome 19 (C19MC), demethylation of the ELF5 promoter, and the expression of GATA3, TFAP2C, and KRT7 proteins [ ]. This approach enabled the derivation of pTSCs from dermal fibroblasts, providing a non-invasive and practical method for establishing pTSCs. A recent study examined whether naïve or primed iPSCs are more suitable for producing pTSCs that accurately model placental disorders ( ). Morey et al. demonstrated that both naïve- and primed-derived iPSCs from PE patients efficiently generated pTSCs [ ]. However, EVTs differentiated from primed iPSC-TSCs, but not from naïve iPSC-TSCs, exhibited pathological characteristics of PE, including reduced surface HLA-G expression, impaired invasiveness, and altered EVT-specific gene expression [ ]. These abnormalities correlated with hypermethylation of promoters of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suggesting that aberrant epigenetic regulation may contribute to the pathogenesis of PE. These findings indicate that primed iPSCs may be more appropriate for modeling PE through conversion into pTSCs. However, as shown in some earlier studies [ , ], primed iPSC-TSCs were deficient in C19MC expression, and the analysis was limited to DNA methylation without examining chromatin accessibility or other epigenetic modifications. This indicates that further research is necessary before firm conclusions can be drawn. Notably, in this study, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from umbilical cords were reprogrammed into iPSCs and subsequently converted into hTSCs. The use of umbilical cords, which retain genetic and epigenetic information from both parents, offers a significant advantage over skin, peripheral blood, or other tissues for modeling placental disorders. Importantly, iPSCs and iPSC-derived pTSCs derived from placental or fetal cells enable isogenic modeling of both placental and embryonic development. Nevertheless, multistep protocols, prolonged conversion durations, and low overall conversion efficiency remain major challenges for the application of iPSC-derived pTSCs. pTSCs directly reprogrammed from fibroblasts via TF induction (fibroblast-derived pTSCs) pTSCs can also be directly reprogrammed from fibroblasts through ectopic expression of TFs. Liu et al. demonstrated that during the reprogramming of human dermal fibroblasts into iPSCs via the introduction of OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC (OSKM), a subset of cells enters a TE-like state. By capturing and culturing this cell population in TSCM, they derived stable induced TSCs (iTSCs) [ ]. iTSCs expressed key markers of human TE and TSCs, including P63, TFAP2C, GATA2, and KRT7, and were capable of differentiating into STs and EVTs. This study was the first to demonstrate that iTSCs can be directly derived from human somatic cells without an intermediate iPSC stage. Subsequently, Castel et al. confirmed that OSKM reprogramming of dermal fibroblasts, including neonatal fibroblasts, can generate iTSCs whose transcriptomes closely resemble those of post-implantation day 8 CTs [ ]. These findings indicate that iTSCs offer a useful platform for studying early post-implantation trophoblast development. While OSKM overexpression in mouse fibroblasts can activate an initial trophoblast-like transcriptional program during iPSC generation, it does not lead to the establishment of stable iTSCs [ , ], suggesting an intriguing species-specific difference. Notably, stable iTSCs can be generated from mouse fibroblasts through the ectopic expression of TFs, such as Gata3, Eomes, Tfap2c, and either Myc or Ets2 (GETM/GETE) [ , ]. Notably, stable iTSCs can be generated from mouse fibroblasts through the ectopic expression of TFs, such as Gata3, Eomes, Tfap2c, and either Myc or Ets2 (GETM/GETE) [ , ]. Fogarty et al. demonstrated that the pluripotency factor OCT4 plays a role in trophoblast lineage induction, as OCT4-null human embryos exhibited downregulation of extra-embryonic TE genes such as CDX2 [ ]. Comparative parallel multi-omic analyses subsequently revealed that the molecular trajectories leading to pluripotent and trophoblast states during OSKM reprogramming are distinct in mice [ , ], raising the question of whether a pluripotent state is necessary for human iTSC induction. Notably, the generation of stable iTSCs from mouse fibroblasts through the expression of Gata3-containing TF cocktails is achieved independently of pluripotency [ , ]. Naama et al. demonstrated that ectopic expression of GOKM (replacing SOX2 with GATA3 in OSKM) can also reprogram human fibroblasts into functional hTSCs [ ]. GOKM efficiently generated iTSCs from fibroblasts lacking pluripotency genes, suggesting that pluripotency is dispensable for acquiring the hTSC state. Mechanistic and transcriptional analyses revealed that GOKM primarily targets hTSC-specific loci, whereas OSKM induces the iTSC state by acting on loci shared between hESCs and hTSCs. Notably, OSKM-derived iTSCs aberrantly expressed 94 hTSC-specific genes compared to GOKM-derived iTSCs [ ]. Furthermore, OSKM-derived iTSCs lacked gene signatures associated with estrogen response and immune function, critical processes for implantation and early placental development [ – ]. This study underscored the importance of selecting the appropriate TFs for directly inducing pTSCs from fibroblasts while preserving functional competence. Patient-derived iTSCs offer a unique platform for investigating early placental developmental defects and disorders in genetically diverse patient populations. In mouse systems, the direct conversion of fibroblasts into iTSCs has been suggested to be superior to derivation from pluripotent cells, which can lead to unstable colonies and epigenetic abnormalities [ ]. This advantage may stem from the fact that conversion to iTSCs occurs through a single, lineage-directed step rather than a two-step process. However, iTSC induction still involves epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling, which may compromise epigenetic fidelity [ ]. Importantly, pTSCs derived from maternal somatic cell types do not capture biparental genetic contributions, underscoring the need to consider the cell of origin when deriving pTSCs from iPSCs or fibroblasts ( ). pTSCs derived from CTs after pregnancy completion (CT-derived pTSCs) The direct derivation of hTSCs from primary CTs offers significant advantages for preserving the genetic and epigenetic features of a patient’s placenta. Saha et al. reported the establishment of hTSCs from first-trimester CTs obtained from patients with idiopathic RPLs (RPL-TSCs) [ ]. After initial passages on placental mesenchymal stromal feeders, RPL-TSCs could be maintained in feeder-free conditions and retained normal karyotypes. These cells exhibited reduced proliferation, unstable morphology, and inefficient organoid formation, all of which were restored after the rescue of TEAD4 expression [ ]. This study demonstrated that pTSCs can be established from placental tissues of patients with idiopathic RPL and they effectively model molecular abnormalities not observed in bona fide hTSCs. Early placentas in cases of idiopathic RPL still retain TSCM-responsive villous CT populations. However, Okae and others were unable to derive hTSCs or trophoblast organoids from term placentas using the culture conditions applied to first-trimester samples [ , , ], suggesting that establishing hTSCs from term placentas may require alternative approaches. Bai et al. achieved this by forced expression of CDX2, ELF5, ETS2, TFAP2C, and TEAD4 in villous CTs isolated from term placentas at birth and cultured in a modified TSCM [ ]. The derived iTSCs exhibit transcriptional similarity to hTSCs, can self-renew indefinitely, and are bipotent. Wang et al. also derived hTSCs from term placentas under 1% oxygen in TSCM that exhibited key properties of bona fide hTSCs [ ]. More recently, Karakis et al. derived hTSCs from CTs isolated at delivery using TSCM supplemented with the low-dose mitochondrial pyruvate uptake inhibitor UK5099 and lipid-rich albumin (TUA) [ ]. The addition of lipid-rich albumin enabled long-term culture but produced cells lacking differentiation potential. Only with additional UK5099 supplementation did hTSCs exhibit the capacity to differentiate into EVT and ST lineages [ ]. Similarly, Hoshiyama et al. isolated ITGA6 + CTs from the term smooth chorion and established chorion-derived TSCs (Ch-TSCs) using TSCM [ ]. Ch-TSCs were transcriptionally similar to hTSCs from first-trimester placental villi. However, their transcriptomic profiles differed from those of pTSCs derived by Karakis et al. CT-derived pTSCs allow for the utilization of routinely discarded placentas without the need for further invasive procedures. However, in many placental disorders, trophoblast lineage abnormalities arise early but manifest clinically in mid to late gestation [ ]. Thus, genetic and epigenetic alterations in CT-derived pTSCs may reflect secondary consequences of chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and other pathological conditions rather than primary drivers. Moreover, even in uncomplicated pregnancies, genetic variants in the placenta tend to accumulate over time, and clones harboring advantageous mutations may expand rapidly [ , ]. These factors complicate causal inference and limit the use of CT-derived pTSCs for investigating the pathogenesis of placental disorders. While functional and mechanistic findings from CT-derived pTSCs are applicable to subsequent pregnancies, their utility for individual risk stratification, prognostic prediction, and personalized therapeutic approaches may be limited for patients without plans for future pregnancies. pTSCs derived from chorionic villi collected via CVS (CV-derived pTSCs) CVS is a prenatal diagnostic procedure that obtains placental tissue to assess fetal chromosomal abnormalities and genetic disorders, typically performed between 10 and 13 weeks of gestation [ ]. Varberg et al. established chorionic villus-derived hTSCs (CV-TSCs) during ongoing pregnancy by culturing freshly isolated villus tissue in TSCM, followed by prolonged culture in a modified TSCM [ ]. In clinical CVS procedures, the median quantity of chorionic villi generally ranges from 20 to 50 mg [ – ]. A minimum of 5 mg of chorionic villus tissue is required to provide sufficient material for karyotype analysis [ – ]. Consequently, residual tissue not required for diagnostic purposes may be utilized for CV-TSC derivation. Varberg et al. established CV-TSC lines from 5–10 mg of residual chorionic villus tissue and reported an induction efficiency of 42% [ ]. The ability to derive CV-TSCs from early placentas has significant implications for both research and clinical translation. First, CV-TSCs are considered to faithfully reflect the genetic status of early-pregnancy trophoblasts [ ], allowing for an evaluation of whether genetic abnormalities are a causal factor or a secondary consequence in placental disorders. Second, CV-TSCs can be obtained from early pregnancies without termination and can be prospectively linked to longitudinal data on the occurrence of placental disorders, related phenotypic outcomes, and even post-natal fetal development [ ]. Clinical information, such as the timing of onset and severity of subsequent placental disorders, can be collected from ongoing pregnancies after the establishment of pTSCs and integrated with the characteristics of these cells. As the interval from CVS specimen collection to evaluating the differentiation potential of CV-TSC lines is approximately three months [ ], current applications are more realistically suited for disease stratification, mechanistic studies, and potentially retrospective analyses rather than for real-time diagnostic use. As CVS is performed as a diagnostic test when a fetus is considered at high risk for chromosomal abnormalities or genetic disorders [ ], it is associated with fewer ethical concerns [ ]. The amount of chorionic villus tissue collected via CVS represents only about 0.008–0.10% of the average placental weight at the time of the procedure [ , , ]. Furthermore, CVS is conducted under ultrasound guidance, and the risk of procedure-related pregnancy loss is estimated to be around 0.2–0.3% [ , , ]. Compared to amniocentesis , which is generally performed from 15 weeks of gestation, CVS offers an earlier opportunity for prenatal diagnosis [ ]. Importantly, CVS should not be performed for research purpose, and derivation of CV-TSC lines should be restricted to residual tissue obtained from clinically indicated procedures. The partial allocation of clinical specimens for research may reduce the available sample volume for diagnosis, potentially leading to inaccurate or inconclusive clinical results. Therefore, the derivation of pTSCs from CVS specimens requires strict adherence to established protocols and regulatory standards, including institutional review board (IRB) approval, prior informed consent, and careful management of specimen division and traceability. Given the availability of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), CVS should not be performed without a clear clinical indication [ ]. Given the availability of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), CVS should not be performed without a clear clinical indication [ ]. Prospective applications of pTSCs To date, hTSCs have primarily been derived from healthy cells and tissues; however, future efforts focused on establishing pTSCs from patient-derived placental tissues will be important. Studies on RPL and PE-derived pTSCs already demonstrated that pTSC-based platforms can deliver meaningful molecular and functional readouts in disorder-relevant settings [ , ]. Saha et al. established pTSCs by isolating CTs from post-miscarriage placental tissues of patients with unexplained RPL, showing that reduced TEAD4 expression is associated with diminished self-renewal. Furthermore, restoring TEAD4 expression rescued this self-renewal defect [ ]. Morey et al. derived naïve and primed iPSCs from postpartum placentas of patients with PE and generated pTSCs through trans-differentiation, which they used to identify epigenetic defects during EVT differentiation [ ]. Collectively, pTSCs are increasingly leveraged to elucidate the molecular underpinnings and pathogenic mechanisms of various placental disorders [ , ]. A practical next step in extending pTSCs for clinical diagnosis and therapeutic applications is to establish a standardized panel of endpoints across various pTSC sources. This panel should include: (1) ST/EVT differentiation efficiency; (2) functional validation through EVT invasion, ST barrier leakage, and hormone secretion assays; and (3) transcriptomic and epigenomic reference mapping. A systematic comparison of pTSC lines may clarify the factors driving clonal variability among hTSCs, which could stem from differences in clinical contexts, tissue origin and quality, derivation and culture methods, or underlying genetic and epigenetic backgrounds. The establishment and preservation of pTSC biobanks will allow for repeated and expanded analyses from the same resource, unlike conventional biobanks that rely on biospecimens available in limited quantities [ ], providing a critical foundation for future research. CV-TSCs, in particular, can be obtained before the onset of placental disorders and are notable for their capacity to collect additional clinical specimens and data prospectively. Placental disorders causing major outcomes can be assessed within months, while long-term follow-up enables multilayered analyses linking postpartum maternal health, neonatal neurodevelopment, and a wide range of other outcomes [ ]. This could evolve into a novel prospective cohort study leveraging pTSCs. The characteristics of pTSCs can be assessed alongside clinical data such as lifestyle information, blood test results, imaging data, placental pathology, and multi-omics profiles, facilitating a mechanistic understanding of gene-regulatory mechanisms. This offers a complementary approach to current precision medicine and lays the groundwork for personalized strategies in diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Incorporating pTSCs into trophoblast organoids or placenta-on-a-chip platforms will enhance their physiological relevance and accelerate translational research by enabling mechanistic studies of placental disorder pathogenesis, evaluation of drug responses, screening of therapeutic candidates, and development of gene-based interventions. Trophoblast organoids derived from naïve hPSC-derived TSCs have been shown to replicate the dynamics of the X chromosome inactivation in the placenta and also demonstrate selective vulnerability to both SARS-CoV-2 and the Zika virus [ ]. Successful clinical translation of cell and gene therapies will require process designs that prioritize manufacturability and the implementation of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)-based quality systems [ ]. Integrating automation, rigorous validation, and regulatory compliance into standard operating procedures will be critical to success. These advances are expected to strengthen translational pipelines, shifting the traditional one-way trajectory from bedside to bench toward a truly bidirectional paradigm. It is important to note that the efficiency and duration of derivation, reproducibility, and the resulting cell states and functional readouts can vary depending on the starting material and derivation protocols. While CV-TSC lines can be established before delivery, the current window for derivation and functional evaluation extends beyond early gestation, a period during which significant placental development occurs. Additional bottlenecks may include inter- and intra-placental heterogeneity, assay and batch effects, as well as genetic and epigenetic drift that can occur during the prolonged culture of pTSCs. Concluding remarks pTSCs are emerging as an innovative platform driving advances in placental biology and reproductive medicine. They can be established through various approaches, including the trans-differentiation of iPSCs, direct reprogramming from fibroblasts, derivation from CTs after pregnancy completion, and from chorionic villi collected via CVS during pregnancy. CV-TSCs hold particular promise, as they can be obtained from early placental tissue without terminating the pregnancy, allowing for longitudinal studies with prospective clinical datasets. Retaining each patient’s unique genetic and epigenetic backgrounds, pTSCs enable investigations into placental disorder pathogenesis, prediction of individual risk, and the development of personalized therapies. Multiple complementary sources of pTSCs provide powerful toolkits for modeling placental development and disorders. Although there have been numerous reports on hTSC derivation from diverse starting materials and distinct media and TF combinations, the field lacks thorough head-to-head benchmarking. Systematic comparisons across protocols, particularly via transcriptional and epigenomic alignment through bona fide placental CTs, along with the standardization of derivation protocols and differentiation state assessment, will be a key priority. Comparative analyses across pTSC models can help disentangle primary pathogenic mechanisms from secondary adaptations, reveal genotype-epigenotype-phenotype relationships, and facilitate mechanistic dissection across distinct developmental windows. Looking ahead, advances in the field will rely on the standardization of derivation protocols, comparative studies across diverse patient populations, systematic genomic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic profiling, and the establishment of pTSC biobanks. Together, these efforts will address current knowledge gaps (see ) and allow pTSCs to evolve from simple experimental models into indispensable resources for precision medicine in reproductive health, expanding our understanding of placental disorders and supporting patient-specific approaches for the diagnosis, prevention, and management of pregnancy complications.

chunks.content: Introduction An obstetrical ultrasound examination provides invaluable information about the fetus. In early pregnancy, it is important to confirm viability, establish gestational age accurately, determine the number of fetuses, and assess both chorionicity and amnionicity for a multiple pregnancy . However, with advancements in ultrasound resolution, there has been a gradual shift in the role of early pregnancy ultrasounds from primarily serving a screening function to also encompassing diagnostic capabilities for identifying structural abnormalities. A cohort study has indicated that the incidence rate of fetal structural abnormalities is approximately 3.0%, with 43.1% of these anomalies detectable in early pregnancy . The introduction of nuchal translucency (NT) aneuploidy screening during the 11 to 13 + 6 weeks further arouses interest in early anatomical scanning . The ultrasound examination carried out according to a standardized protocol can maximize its value and increase the detection rate of fetal abnormalities , . Therefore, the process of quality control for the early ultrasound scan between 11 and 13 + 6 weeks is essential for fetal defects detection at this stage. However, the implementation of large-scale quality control faces substantial demands on manpower and time. Moreover, inter-observer variability frequently undermines the reliability of the results, presenting a further challenge to its popularization , . In recent years, a growing body of researches have applied artificial intelligence (AI) to obstetric ultrasound, enabling the rapid and repeatable analysis of fetal ultrasound images through innovative methods. Studies have successfully applied AI to identify fetal structures, perform measurements of fetal biometry, and even make intelligent diagnoses , . Besides, several methods for intelligent quality assessment of fetal ultrasound images have been proposed – . Although promising, most existing studies are limited to mid- or late- pregnancy and focus only on biometric or cardiac planes. Consequently, they are inapplicable to first-trimester scans and insufficient for comprehensive intelligent quality control throughout the entire scanning process. In this study, we collaborated with the ultrasound department of the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University and AIRIGIN company to develop an First Trimester Ultrasound Quality-control System (FUQS) according to the recognized guideline in China, Chinese expert consensus on assessment standards of obstetric ultrasound training program (2022 edition) . This system was then implemented for the evaluation of first trimester ultrasound examinations in Liaoning Province. Results Image data for FUQS development and test In total, 41,968 images from 7251 pregnancies were enrolled for the development and test of FUQS (Fig. ). Of which, 33,697 images from 6854 pregnancies were collected for model development, including 30,326 images for training and 3371 images for internal testing. Additionally, 8271 images from 300 pregnancies were used for external testing. The details were displayed in Table . Performance of FUQS Identifying the anatomic structures accurately is a prerequisite for the quality audit. Based on the You Only Look Once version 5 (YOLOv5) network trained, we achieved good results in identifying structures from fetal ultrasound images, with a precision of 81.12%, recall of 78.43%, and mean average precision (mAP) of 0.8327 on the internal test dataset. In the task of multi-view clustering -defined as the simultaneous classification of multiple target views- FUQS achieved an overall accuracy of 96.05% based on experts’ decisions. The highest consistency (100%) was found in the transventricular axial view. However the lowest consistency (91.86%) occurred in the abdominal cord insertion view with the most common error being its confusion with the transverse abdominal view. Figure visualized the target view clustering results in the external test dataset. When comparing FUQS and manual scoring, we found a high correlation between FUQS and different experts, with an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.957 ( P < 0.001). The ICC among the three experts was 0.955 ( P < 0.001). We further created violin plots to narrate the differences between FUQS and the average assessment of the three experts quantitatively. We could see the difference value focused more on zero among the eight target views as well as the total score (Fig. ). It took an average of only three seconds for the FUQS to complete the assessment of one examination, significantly shorter than the time required by experts (an average of 63.50 s, P < 0.001). Of these, 22/35 (62.86%) were Tier 3 hospitals, and 13/35 (37.14%) were Tier 2 hospitals. Additionally, 29/35 (82.86%) were general hospitals, while 6/35 (17.14%) were obstetrics-specialized hospitals. The characteristics of the 35 hospitals were detailed in Supplementary Table . Thirty-five ultrasound examinations performed in December 2022 were later randomly selected from each hospital. Finally, a total of 1750 cases were selected in the audit. The overall median number of images saved per case was 19 (Inter-quartile range (IQR) 13–25), with a significant variation among the 1750 cases (ranging from 2 to 87 images, P < 0.001). As shown in Table , the number of images saved differed significantly between Tier 3 and Tier 2 hospitals ( P < 0.001) as well as between general and specialized hospitals ( P < 0.001). Besides, the overall median score was 58.50 (IQR 45.00–72.00) among the hospitals. Tier 3 hospitals had a median score of 62.00 (IQR 47.00–75.00), higher than Tier 2 hospitals with a median score of 52.00 (IQR 42.00–66.63); while specialized hospitals had a median score of 75.00 (IQR 59.00–85.00), outperforming general hospitals, which had a median score of 56.00 (IQR 43.13–69.00) (Table and Fig. ). The overall scan completion rate for the required views was 65.85%. We further summarized the completion rates for individual views. The rates were higher for the midsagittal view of fetus (99.43%), the transventricular axial view (91.31%), and the NT measurement view (89.37%). In contrast, the completion rates were lower for the abdominal cord insertion view (32.69%), the four-chamber view (34.23%), and the transverse abdominal view (40.57%). Moreover, manual large-scale quality control is labor-intensive and time-consuming, with potential issues in reproducibility and reliance on subjective judgments. In this study, following the established guidelines in China, we successfully developed an AI-driven quality control system for first-trimester ultrasound examinations. Furthermore, this system was effectively implemented for first-trimester ultrasound quality control in Liaoning Province. Our model provides a comprehensive evaluation of first-trimester ultrasound examinations, including detailed scoring of the ultrasound scan and a checklist to ensure completeness. Additionally, it represents a breakthrough in quality control practice by offering an objective method to assess numerous examinations with reduced time requirements. Moreover, the intelligent system could also be applied in the process of qualification and accreditation. As one of the largest provinces in China, Liaoning Province has a diverse range of hospitals practicing obstetric ultrasound, which presents challenge for maintaining audit quality. This study represents the quality audit of the first trimester ultrasound examinations conducted by an official organization, supported by local governments and health committees. With the assistance of FUQS, we gained a better understanding of the current situation regarding fetal scans. As reported, increased fetal NT thickness during the first trimester is a common phenotypic expression of fetal chromosomal defects, structural abnormalities, and genetic syndromes . The accuracy of the measurement critically depends on the quality of the ultrasound view; therefore, the NT measurement view is considered the most important during the examination. Despite a high completion rate of 89.37% for this critical view, lower detection rates of the nasal bone or nasal tip are the primary reasons for the reduced excellent rate. Additionally, the absence of fetal nasal bone is an independent characteristic associated with the first-trimester screening for trisomy 21 , . Therefore, it is crucial to emphasize the importance of nasal bone detection. The midsagittal view of fetus is another important view of the ultrasound examination at this stage, as the measurement of crown-rump length in this view is considered the most reliable method for establishing gestational age . The midsagittal view of fetus achieved a high completion rate of 99.43%; however, the excellent rate was only 38.29%. This lower excellent rate is attributed to the failure to detect the nasal bone or nasal tip, as well as the inability to show the full length of the spine. Among the target views, the abdominal cord insertion view and the four-chamber view exhibited the lowest completion rate of 32.69% and 34.23% respectively, which should be taken seriously. The abdominal cord insertion view is important for observing the integrity of the anterior abdominal wall and diagnosing omphalocele, which may be associated with chromosomal abnormalities . In addition, first-trimester ultrasound examination of the fetal heart allows for the identification of over half of the fetuses affected by major cardiac defects, moreover the use of color-flow Doppler in the four-chamber view assessment is independently associated with a significantly higher rate of detection ( P < 0.001) . Therefore, enhancing the completeness of the four-chamber view significantly boosts the detection rate of major cardiac abnormalities in the first trimester. Moreover, our data reveals that Tier 3 hospitals outperformed Tier 2 hospitals, and specialized hospitals performed better than general hospitals. This underscores the need for Tier 3 hospitals to maintain their leadership role and for general hospitals to enhance their prenatal ultrasound scanning practices. As demonstrated, FUQS represents an effective tool for quality control in ultrasound practice. Building on these findings, future efforts will focus on broadening its impact through two primary pathways: geographical expansion to more regions for protocol optimization, and integration into clinical training to systematically enhance scanning quality following a structured feedback mechanism for participating hospitals and sonographers. However, our quality control system still has some limitations. Firstly, all images used for training or testing were obtained from fetuses without structural defects, indicating that the tool’s efficacy in assessing fetuses with defects has not yet been evaluated. Increasing the sample size in subsequent studies could provide a more comprehensive evaluation. In conclusion, we have successfully developed a systematic quality audit system for first trimester ultrasound examination, and it was applied to the quality control practice in Liaoning Province. The AI-based quality audit system provides rapid, objective, and repeatable evaluations. Beyond assessing overall performance, our model provides detailed scores for each view, thereby assisting in pinpointing weaknesses in scanning with reduced time consumption. Furthermore, providing feedback to participants may further enhance the quality of their scanning. The application of FUQS could serve as an effective tool for quality control practice and skill advancement elevation for physicians. Methods Study design and participants In this multi-center study, we developed, tested, and applied an intelligent model, FUQS, designed to evaluate the quality of fetal ultrasound examinations in first trimester. Furthermore, we assessed the performance of first-trimester ultrasound scans of medical institutions at all levels in Liaoning Province, China, with the assistance of FUQS. Fetal anatomical ultrasound images of participants at a gestational age of 11 to 13 + 6 weeks were collected from the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University between January 2017 and December 2022 to train the FUQS. The external test dataset included fetal ultrasound images stored during routine clinical work at Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University from January 2022 to December 2022. All fetuses included were confirmed to have no evident morphological abnormalities after birth. The quality control survey was conducted in hospitals that provide prenatal screening services in Liaoning Province of China. Initially, we randomly selected 10% of Tier 3 and Tier 2 hospitals respectively for inclusion in the quality audit program. (Chinese hospitals are classified into three Tiers based on scale and technical capabilities, with Tier 1 hospitals not offering prenatal ultrasound screening). We then randomly selected 50 first-trimester (11 to 13 + 6 weeks) ultrasound examinations performed in December 2022 from each hospital. This study was done in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The use of ultrasound images, clinical information, and data collection protocols was approved by the ethics committee of Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University (2017PS264K). As this study involved a retrospective analysis of pre-existing, de-identified data, patient consent was waived by the ethics committee. All data were handled with strict measures to ensure anonymity and protect patient privacy. Procedures Raw data were routinely saved during fetal ultrasound scans and extracted in JPEG format. Ultrasounds were performed transabdominally for pregnancies using various machines, including the GE Voluson 730 Expert/E6/E8/E10, Samsung UGEO WS80A, and Philips EPIQ7C. All images were obtained by various operators, each with more than five years of independent fetal diagnostic experience. We divided the image dataset into standard views and other views. Standard views included all the views required to be saved according to the practice guideline recognized across China , while other views comprised those not required to be saved by the guidelines but were frequently captured during the scanning process. The training images were assigned randomly into training, validation, and internal test dataset at a ratio of approximately 8:1:1. Then, the images were labeled using the annotation tool LabelImg. The data annotation process was conducted by a seven-person team consisting of four resident physicians (with five years of independent fetal diagnostic experience) for initial labeling, two superior physicians (with ten years of independent fetal diagnostic experience) to further check and adjust the labels, and one experienced physician (with 20 years of independent fetal diagnostic experience) to recheck the labels finally. the images were labeled using the annotation tool LabelImg. The data annotation process was conducted by a seven-person team consisting of four resident physicians (with five years of independent fetal diagnostic experience) for initial labeling, two superior physicians (with ten years of independent fetal diagnostic experience) to further check and adjust the labels, and one experienced physician (with 20 years of independent fetal diagnostic experience) to recheck the labels finally. All images (both standard and other views) were labeled with a total of 240 annotations in the form of rectangular bounding boxes, including irrelevant information such as machine parameters, image types (single or double views), image location (left or right view for the image with double views), and specific structures assigned to the model. To make the algorithm robust, the training dataset was further augmented threefold before training using CutMix, Crop, Paste, Horizontal/Vertical flip, Rotation, and HSV(Hue, Saturation, Value) color jitter. After augmentation, all images were resized from the original scales into the uniform size of 640 × 640 pixels. The development of FUQS The algorithm we developed was based on YOLOv5, a state-of-the-art object detection framework. YOLOv5 is one of the fastest algorithm for image recognition in the AI field and has been extensively studied in areas such as industry and agriculture . Although research on its application in medicine is relatively rare, it could prove to be a valuable tool for detecting and classifying tasks in fetal ultrasound images, offering rapid and accurate assessments . The input of the model was the fetal ultrasound images stored during a routine first-trimester ultrasound screening. In the first step, the model analyzed the images from the exam, detecting the key structures within each specific ultrasound images. The second step involved a logical network that utilized prior clinical knowledge (the guidelines) to infer possible view classification results along with corresponding scores. Specifically, the logical network matched each target view against all the eight standard views. This ensured that its key structures were captured in the detection network’s predictions, and the frame was classified as the view with the highest probability. For each image, a score was calculated by summing the scores of the detected structures according to the standard set by the guideline. Subsequently, the third step incorporated an additional view clustering method, a combinatorial optimization algorithm, to address the assignment problem for the target views. Specifically, the algorithm began with the initial image and iteratively optimizes the view clustering results to find the optimal view decision based on the scoring. Then the algorithm iteratively improves the matching by exploring augmenting paths until an optimal solution is reached, achieving maximum matching in a weighted bipartite selection. This effectively pairs items from two sets (target views and specific ultrasound images) to maximize the total score. For each examination, the total score was treated as the sum of each views. Finally, the output results included a checklist of the standard views, along with scores for each view and for the entire examination. The model generated a predictive score between 0 and the maximum value for each view, giving a total score for an integral scan of 100. Note that if some of the standard planes were missing during the ultrasound scan, the corresponding views were scored zero points due to the lack of matching views. The model is illustrated in Fig. . The network was trained with stochastic gradient descent using an initial learning rate of 0.01, a momentum of 0.93, and a weight decay of 3 × 10 −4 . The batch size was set to 312 on 8 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080Ti GPUs. The model was trained for 710 epochs, and the optimal model was selected by the loss of validation set of segmentation. FUQS, First Trimester Ultrasound Quality-control System. Statistical analysis The detection performance of the model was first evaluated on internal datasets using precision, recall, and mAP. Intersection over Union (IoU) was employed to quantify the spatial overlap between the ground truth annotation (A) and the model-predicted region (B). An IoU of 1 indicates perfect overlap between A and B, while an IoU of 0 indicates no overlap. In this study, the IoU threshold was set at 0.50. A detection was considered a true positive (TP) if the IoU between A and B exceeded 0.50; a false negative (FN) if the IoU was below 0.50; and a false positive (FP) if a prediction B had no corresponding ground truth A. Based on the counts of TP, FP, and FN, precision and recall were calculated as TP/(TP + FP) and TP/(TP + FN), respectively. The average precision (AP) was determined as the area under the precision-recall curve, and mAP was computed as the mean AP across all target views. We further used the excellent rate and pass rate to assess the performance of the integral examination as well as the performance of different views. It mediates nutrient and gas exchange at the maternal-fetal interface, regulates immune responses, and produces hormones for maintaining pregnancy [ ]. The human placenta consists of three types of trophoblast cells. Cytotrophoblasts ( CTs , see Glossary) are the highly proliferative stem cell population that can give rise to further differentiated syncytiotrophoblasts (STs) and extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs) [ ]. Abnormal placental function can lead to significant obstetric complications, including recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) , preeclampsia (PE) , fetal growth restriction (FGR), and placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) [ ]. Placental research is essential for understanding the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of pregnancy-related complications. Although access to human placental tissue is crucial for studying placental development and function, its acquisition and use have been limited by technical and ethical challenges [ , ]. Given the limited availability of early-stage human placental tissue, various in vitro models have been developed to investigate placental development, function, and the maintenance of pregnancy ( ). By adapting the established derivation and culture protocols by Okae et al. [ ], patient-specific trophoblast stem cells (pTSCs) have been generated from various sources, including human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), somatic fibroblasts, CTs obtained after completed pregnancies, and more recently, chorionic villus tissue obtained via chorionic villus sampling (CVS) during ongoing pregnancies ( ). pTSCs can retain the genetic and epigenetic abnormalities of individual pregnancies. By capturing inter-individual genetic diversity, research using pTSCs offers powerful tools for understanding placental development and the pathogenesis of pregnancy-related complications. Although pTSCs are emerging as key models for studying placental development and disorders, their derivation methods have not yet been comprehensively reviewed. In this review, we underscore the importance of pTSCs, evaluate their derivation methods, and provide insights into their applications. The need for pTSCs Placental development and the onset of related disorders are often closely associated with genomic alterations, including gene mutations, chromosomal abnormalities, and changes in transcriptomic and epigenomic signatures [ , ]. Many placental disorders exhibit distinct manifestations influenced by genetic background, immune responses, and environmentally driven epigenetic variation [ – ]. An analysis of the transcriptomic landscape in monosomy X placentas highlights the impact of chromosomal abnormalities on early placental development, suggesting that attenuated cytokine-signaling pathways affect immune regulation [ ]. Placentas with large-scale aneuploidies or copy-number variations (CNVs) are more frequently associated with small-for-gestational-age infants compared to karyotypically normal placentas [ ]. Such complexity is challenging to capture or interrogate using the limited number of available bona fide hTSC lines, which do not fully reflect genetic diversity or the broader transcriptomic and epigenomic landscapes ( ). Relying on these restricted models may undermine their physiological and clinical relevance, as well as the fidelity required to elucidate pathogenesis, predict individual risk, and develop personalized therapeutic strategies. In contrast, patient-specific models can be derived through reprogramming or direct induction from an individual’s cells, reflecting the patient’s genetic and epigenetic backgrounds. While disease-specific models are often developed with a focus on a particular condition [ ], patient-specific stem cells can maintain inter-individual variation even among patients with the same disease. They serve as valuable research models for mechanistic dissection, risk stratification, and therapy development by generating personalized placental models [ , ]. These models offer a precise and reproducible system that allows for systematic analysis of disorder-associated alterations in trophoblast proliferation, differentiation, invasiveness, and immune regulation. Even in the presence of the same mutation, inter-individual genetic and epigenetic differences can lead to varying degrees of cellular dysfunction [ , ]. By leveraging pTSCs, inter-individual differences in susceptibility to placental disorders can be evaluated in vitro . Certain pTSC-based approaches also alleviate ethical concerns and enable longitudinal follow-up of clinical outcomes ( ) ( ). This positions pTSCs as key platforms for placental disease research, patient-specific risk assessment, and therapy. pTSC derivation pTSCs can be generated via : (1) trans-differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) reprogrammed from patient somatic cells; (2) direct reprogramming from fibroblasts by forced expression of transcription factors (TFs); (3) derivation from CTs after the completion of pregnancy; and (4) derivation from chorionic villi collected via CVS during early pregnancy ( ). pTSCs trans-differentiated from iPSCs (iPSC-derived pTSCs) Earlier attempts at pTSC derivation involved reprogramming somatic cells into iPSCs, followed by trans-differentiation into hTSCs. Dong et al. reported that when naïve human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) or renal epithelial cell-derived iPSCs are cultured in hTSC medium (TSCM), a homogeneous cell population closely resembling bona fide hTSCs is produced, exhibiting similar gross morphology, surface markers, and trophoblast-specific gene expression [ ]. However, this model did not fully recapitulate the developmental continuum from pre-implantation to post-implantation stages, as cells representing the initial trophoblast lineage, trophectoderm (TE) , were not detected during the conversion of iPSCs into pTSCs. iPSC-derived pTSCs (iPSC-TSCs) were transcriptionally most similar to the human post-implantation TE lineage at day 12, with low levels of CDX2 [ ], a TF that is markedly downregulated in CTs as the first trimester progresses [ ]. In parallel, Cinkornpumin et al. showed that naïve hPSCs can be converted to hTSCs [ ]. In addition, their findings indicated substantial differences in conversion efficiency, lineage fidelity, and differentiation capacity of the TSCs, depending on the PSC state and cell lines. Shortly after, Io et al. induced pTSCs that more closely resemble pre-implantation-stage TE from naïve hESCs and iPSCs using the ACE culture condition, which contains A83–01, CHIR99021, and epidermal growth factor (EGF) [ ]. This method established an in vitro model that faithfully recapitulates the complete trajectory of trophoblast development from pre- to post-implantation. The derived pTSCs have met established criteria for human first-trimester trophoblasts, including extended self-renewal, bipotency, lack of HLA class I expression, an active miRNA cluster on chromosome 19 (C19MC), demethylation of the ELF5 promoter, and the expression of GATA3, TFAP2C, and KRT7 proteins [ ]. This approach enabled the derivation of pTSCs from dermal fibroblasts, providing a non-invasive and practical method for establishing pTSCs. A recent study examined whether naïve or primed iPSCs are more suitable for producing pTSCs that accurately model placental disorders ( ). Morey et al. demonstrated that both naïve- and primed-derived iPSCs from PE patients efficiently generated pTSCs [ ]. However, EVTs differentiated from primed iPSC-TSCs, but not from naïve iPSC-TSCs, exhibited pathological characteristics of PE, including reduced surface HLA-G expression, impaired invasiveness, and altered EVT-specific gene expression [ ]. These abnormalities correlated with hypermethylation of promoters of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suggesting that aberrant epigenetic regulation may contribute to the pathogenesis of PE. These findings indicate that primed iPSCs may be more appropriate for modeling PE through conversion into pTSCs. However, as shown in some earlier studies [ , ], primed iPSC-TSCs were deficient in C19MC expression, and the analysis was limited to DNA methylation without examining chromatin accessibility or other epigenetic modifications. This indicates that further research is necessary before firm conclusions can be drawn. Notably, in this study, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from umbilical cords were reprogrammed into iPSCs and subsequently converted into hTSCs. The use of umbilical cords, which retain genetic and epigenetic information from both parents, offers a significant advantage over skin, peripheral blood, or other tissues for modeling placental disorders. Importantly, iPSCs and iPSC-derived pTSCs derived from placental or fetal cells enable isogenic modeling of both placental and embryonic development. Nevertheless, multistep protocols, prolonged conversion durations, and low overall conversion efficiency remain major challenges for the application of iPSC-derived pTSCs. pTSCs directly reprogrammed from fibroblasts via TF induction (fibroblast-derived pTSCs) pTSCs can also be directly reprogrammed from fibroblasts through ectopic expression of TFs. Liu et al. demonstrated that during the reprogramming of human dermal fibroblasts into iPSCs via the introduction of OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC (OSKM), a subset of cells enters a TE-like state. By capturing and culturing this cell population in TSCM, they derived stable induced TSCs (iTSCs) [ ]. iTSCs expressed key markers of human TE and TSCs, including P63, TFAP2C, GATA2, and KRT7, and were capable of differentiating into STs and EVTs. This study was the first to demonstrate that iTSCs can be directly derived from human somatic cells without an intermediate iPSC stage. Subsequently, Castel et al. confirmed that OSKM reprogramming of dermal fibroblasts, including neonatal fibroblasts, can generate iTSCs whose transcriptomes closely resemble those of post-implantation day 8 CTs [ ]. These findings indicate that iTSCs offer a useful platform for studying early post-implantation trophoblast development. Fogarty et al. demonstrated that the pluripotency factor OCT4 plays a role in trophoblast lineage induction, as OCT4-null human embryos exhibited downregulation of extra-embryonic TE genes such as CDX2 [ ]. Comparative parallel multi-omic analyses subsequently revealed that the molecular trajectories leading to pluripotent and trophoblast states during OSKM reprogramming are distinct in mice [ , ], raising the question of whether a pluripotent state is necessary for human iTSC induction. Notably, the generation of stable iTSCs from mouse fibroblasts through the expression of Gata3-containing TF cocktails is achieved independently of pluripotency [ , ]. Naama et al. demonstrated that ectopic expression of GOKM (replacing SOX2 with GATA3 in OSKM) can also reprogram human fibroblasts into functional hTSCs [ ]. GOKM efficiently generated iTSCs from fibroblasts lacking pluripotency genes, suggesting that pluripotency is dispensable for acquiring the hTSC state. Mechanistic and transcriptional analyses revealed that GOKM primarily targets hTSC-specific loci, whereas OSKM induces the iTSC state by acting on loci shared between hESCs and hTSCs. Notably, OSKM-derived iTSCs aberrantly expressed 94 hTSC-specific genes compared to GOKM-derived iTSCs [ ]. Furthermore, OSKM-derived iTSCs lacked gene signatures associated with estrogen response and immune function, critical processes for implantation and early placental development [ – ]. This study underscored the importance of selecting the appropriate TFs for directly inducing pTSCs from fibroblasts while preserving functional competence. Patient-derived iTSCs offer a unique platform for investigating early placental developmental defects and disorders in genetically diverse patient populations. In mouse systems, the direct conversion of fibroblasts into iTSCs has been suggested to be superior to derivation from pluripotent cells, which can lead to unstable colonies and epigenetic abnormalities [ ]. This advantage may stem from the fact that conversion to iTSCs occurs through a single, lineage-directed step rather than a two-step process. However, iTSC induction still involves epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling, which may compromise epigenetic fidelity [ ]. Importantly, pTSCs derived from maternal somatic cell types do not capture biparental genetic contributions, underscoring the need to consider the cell of origin when deriving pTSCs from iPSCs or fibroblasts ( ). pTSCs derived from CTs after pregnancy completion (CT-derived pTSCs) The direct derivation of hTSCs from primary CTs offers significant advantages for preserving the genetic and epigenetic features of a patient’s placenta. Saha et al. reported the establishment of hTSCs from first-trimester CTs obtained from patients with idiopathic RPLs (RPL-TSCs) [ ]. After initial passages on placental mesenchymal stromal feeders, RPL-TSCs could be maintained in feeder-free conditions and retained normal karyotypes. These cells exhibited reduced proliferation, unstable morphology, and inefficient organoid formation, all of which were restored after the rescue of TEAD4 expression [ ]. This study demonstrated that pTSCs can be established from placental tissues of patients with idiopathic RPL and they effectively model molecular abnormalities not observed in bona fide hTSCs. Early placentas in cases of idiopathic RPL still retain TSCM-responsive villous CT populations. However, Okae and others were unable to derive hTSCs or trophoblast organoids from term placentas using the culture conditions applied to first-trimester samples [ , , ], suggesting that establishing hTSCs from term placentas may require alternative approaches. Bai et al. achieved this by forced expression of CDX2, ELF5, ETS2, TFAP2C, and TEAD4 in villous CTs isolated from term placentas at birth and cultured in a modified TSCM [ ]. The derived iTSCs exhibit transcriptional similarity to hTSCs, can self-renew indefinitely, and are bipotent. Wang et al. also derived hTSCs from term placentas under 1% oxygen in TSCM that exhibited key properties of bona fide hTSCs [ ]. More recently, Karakis et al. derived hTSCs from CTs isolated at delivery using TSCM supplemented with the low-dose mitochondrial pyruvate uptake inhibitor UK5099 and lipid-rich albumin (TUA) [ ]. Only with additional UK5099 supplementation did hTSCs exhibit the capacity to differentiate into EVT and ST lineages [ ]. CT-derived pTSCs allow for the utilization of routinely discarded placentas without the need for further invasive procedures. However, in many placental disorders, trophoblast lineage abnormalities arise early but manifest clinically in mid to late gestation [ ]. Thus, genetic and epigenetic alterations in CT-derived pTSCs may reflect secondary consequences of chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and other pathological conditions rather than primary drivers. Moreover, even in uncomplicated pregnancies, genetic variants in the placenta tend to accumulate over time, and clones harboring advantageous mutations may expand rapidly [ , ]. These factors complicate causal inference and limit the use of CT-derived pTSCs for investigating the pathogenesis of placental disorders. While functional and mechanistic findings from CT-derived pTSCs are applicable to subsequent pregnancies, their utility for individual risk stratification, prognostic prediction, and personalized therapeutic approaches may be limited for patients without plans for future pregnancies. pTSCs derived from chorionic villi collected via CVS (CV-derived pTSCs) CVS is a prenatal diagnostic procedure that obtains placental tissue to assess fetal chromosomal abnormalities and genetic disorders, typically performed between 10 and 13 weeks of gestation [ ]. Varberg et al. established chorionic villus-derived hTSCs (CV-TSCs) during ongoing pregnancy by culturing freshly isolated villus tissue in TSCM, followed by prolonged culture in a modified TSCM [ ]. In clinical CVS procedures, the median quantity of chorionic villi generally ranges from 20 to 50 mg [ – ]. A minimum of 5 mg of chorionic villus tissue is required to provide sufficient material for karyotype analysis [ – ]. Consequently, residual tissue not required for diagnostic purposes may be utilized for CV-TSC derivation. Varberg et al. established CV-TSC lines from 5–10 mg of residual chorionic villus tissue and reported an induction efficiency of 42% [ ]. The ability to derive CV-TSCs from early placentas has significant implications for both research and clinical translation. First, CV-TSCs are considered to faithfully reflect the genetic status of early-pregnancy trophoblasts [ ], allowing for an evaluation of whether genetic abnormalities are a causal factor or a secondary consequence in placental disorders. Second, CV-TSCs can be obtained from early pregnancies without termination and can be prospectively linked to longitudinal data on the occurrence of placental disorders, related phenotypic outcomes, and even post-natal fetal development [ ]. Clinical information, such as the timing of onset and severity of subsequent placental disorders, can be collected from ongoing pregnancies after the establishment of pTSCs and integrated with the characteristics of these cells. As the interval from CVS specimen collection to evaluating the differentiation potential of CV-TSC lines is approximately three months [ ], current applications are more realistically suited for disease stratification, mechanistic studies, and potentially retrospective analyses rather than for real-time diagnostic use. As CVS is performed as a diagnostic test when a fetus is considered at high risk for chromosomal abnormalities or genetic disorders [ ], it is associated with fewer ethical concerns [ ]. The amount of chorionic villus tissue collected via CVS represents only about 0.008–0.10% of the average placental weight at the time of the procedure [ , , ]. Furthermore, CVS is conducted under ultrasound guidance, and the risk of procedure-related pregnancy loss is estimated to be around 0.2–0.3% [ , , ]. Compared to amniocentesis , which is generally performed from 15 weeks of gestation, CVS offers an earlier opportunity for prenatal diagnosis [ ]. Importantly, CVS should not be performed for research purpose, and derivation of CV-TSC lines should be restricted to residual tissue obtained from clinically indicated procedures. The partial allocation of clinical specimens for research may reduce the available sample volume for diagnosis, potentially leading to inaccurate or inconclusive clinical results. Therefore, the derivation of pTSCs from CVS specimens requires strict adherence to established protocols and regulatory standards, including institutional review board (IRB) approval, prior informed consent, and careful management of specimen division and traceability. Given the availability of non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), CVS should not be performed without a clear clinical indication [ ]. Morey et al. derived naïve and primed iPSCs from postpartum placentas of patients with PE and generated pTSCs through trans-differentiation, which they used to identify epigenetic defects during EVT differentiation [ ]. Collectively, pTSCs are increasingly leveraged to elucidate the molecular underpinnings and pathogenic mechanisms of various placental disorders [ , ]. A practical next step in extending pTSCs for clinical diagnosis and therapeutic applications is to establish a standardized panel of endpoints across various pTSC sources. This panel should include: (1) ST/EVT differentiation efficiency; (2) functional validation through EVT invasion, ST barrier leakage, and hormone secretion assays; and (3) transcriptomic and epigenomic reference mapping. A systematic comparison of pTSC lines may clarify the factors driving clonal variability among hTSCs, which could stem from differences in clinical contexts, tissue origin and quality, derivation and culture methods, or underlying genetic and epigenetic backgrounds. The establishment and preservation of pTSC biobanks will allow for repeated and expanded analyses from the same resource, unlike conventional biobanks that rely on biospecimens available in limited quantities [ ], providing a critical foundation for future research. CV-TSCs, in particular, can be obtained before the onset of placental disorders and are notable for their capacity to collect additional clinical specimens and data prospectively. Placental disorders causing major outcomes can be assessed within months, while long-term follow-up enables multilayered analyses linking postpartum maternal health, neonatal neurodevelopment, and a wide range of other outcomes [ ]. This could evolve into a novel prospective cohort study leveraging pTSCs. The characteristics of pTSCs can be assessed alongside clinical data such as lifestyle information, blood test results, imaging data, placental pathology, and multi-omics profiles, facilitating a mechanistic understanding of gene-regulatory mechanisms. Successful clinical translation of cell and gene therapies will require process designs that prioritize manufacturability and the implementation of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)-based quality systems [ ]. Integrating automation, rigorous validation, and regulatory compliance into standard operating procedures will be critical to success. chunks.content: Introduction Accurate estimated date of delivery (EDD) is helpful for pregnancy outcomes and clinical decisions making , including diagnosing preterm and full-term, formulating measures for fetal dysplasia, arranging the timing of prenatal examination, preparing nursing measures for parturition and improving the efficiency of delivery. A reliable EDD is very important to reduce the occurrence of premature or postmature babies and is critical for both short-term and long-term health outcomes in neonates. Inaccurate EDD may have adverse effects on the health and safety of pregnant women and fetuses. The current clinical method of determining the EDD is based on the information about last menstrual period (LMP) and ultrasound – . Among them, the Naegele’s rule based on LMP is the most common and wide method to calculate the EDD . The Naegele’s rule is calculated by adding seven days and nine months to the first day of the LMP, or the EDD is 280 days after the first day of the LMP. However, the limitations of LMP include deviations in recalling the last menstruation, irregular menstrual cycles, oral contraceptives and early pregnancy bleeding . In several studies, calculating EDD by ultrasound of the first trimester of pregnancy is more accurate than the LMP , . The research of Kessler et al. aimed at assessing the actual pregnancy length and accuracy of EDD prediction based on fetal head circumference measured at the second trimester, a population-based validation of 21,451 deliveries showed measurements can be safely used to predict EDD. Majola et al. compared the accuracy of LMP recall and an early ultrasound (EUS) in predicting the EDD in South African pregnant women, the results show that the effect of using EUS to calculate EDD is obviously better. However, the effect of predicting EDD only using ultrasonic features is not strongly helpful . Interestingly, EDD is also affected by other factors. Obviously, pre pregnancy weight and maternal age are also important factors affecting EDD , . According to Staneva , experiencing psychological distress such as depression, anxiety, and/or perceived stress during pregnancy may increase the risk of preterm birth. In addition, the life and behavior habits during pregnancy also affect EDD , . Besides, some studies believed that the accuracy of EDD will gradually decrease with the increase of gestational weeks . Therefore, the EDD should be determined once we obtain the data from LMP or the first accurate ultrasound examination , . However, some studies showed that only about 5% of births are born exactly on EDD, regardless of the LMP methods or ultrasound . In the study of medical prediction methods, machine learning models are widely used since its high accuracy and high efficiency. Liang et al. used a linear regression model to find the blood metabolites that can predict gestational age and delivery date accurately. Heuvel et al. used convolution neural network (CNN) to estimate fetal head circumference, determine gestational age and delivery date. Fung et al. developed a machine learning approach based on ultrasound-derived and fetal biometric data to estimate gestational age and delivery date, but this article did not mention the type of ML. Schink et al. developed an algorithm to estimate the beginning of pregnancy in German claims data focusing on the potential of the expected delivery date. Torres et al. designed a system to calculate the gestational age and delivery date. They used images from the feet, face and ear of 130 newborn babies and a combination of fully convolutional networks, CNN and support vector regressors (SVR). Kojita et al. used fetal MRI in early pregnancy to predict gestational age and EDD. However, the above-mentioned prediction models ignored the effect of time series factors. Accurate EDD needs to evaluate the physical condition of pregnant women, and analyze the recent trend by judging the fetal development status of pregnant women at all stages. Since the data of antenatal examination is time series data, the EDD is closely related to the results of each examination. Therefore, this study attempted to combine prenatal examination with electronic medical records to establish a hybrid time series model based on Gradient Boosting Decision Tree and Gated Recurrent Unit (GBDT–GRU) to predict the expected date of delivery. A preliminary prediction of EDD was achieved based on data of the first trimester with GBDT model, and considered as a new feature for the prediction of a more precise EDD. The new feature was combined with the original features of the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, and feed into a GRU model to generate the final EDD. Step 4: Results evaluation. The prediction results of EDD with GBDT only, GBDT-GRU hybrid model and other methods were evaluated and compared. Datasets preparation In this study, the data were collected from the electronic medical records (EMR) of pregnant women in a maternity hospital in eastern part of China. We extracted the physical examination and ultrasound records of the pregnant women who natural and full-term delivery between 2017 and 2020. The information was processed in such a way that the individual could not be identified. This study was approved by the ethics committee of Hangzhou Women’s Hospital and performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (written permission with approval NO. 2019-02-2). Considering the necessity of predict EDD in advance, only the physical examination records before 35 weeks were used in this study. The count of physical examinations of pregnant women in different gestational weeks is shown in Fig. . According to Fig. , there are too few pregnancy examinations between 13 and 22 weeks. In addition to the frequency of pregnancy examination, pregnant women have different examination items at different stages of pregnancy. Some ultrasound indicators only appear in the first trimester of pregnancy and will disappear with the increase of pregnancy weeks, such as the gestational sac (e. g, Features of the pregnancy examination Table ). Therefore, we divided the dataset into two subsets according to the time of pregnancy examination: the first trimester of pregnancy dataset (pregnant week: 4 to less than 14 weeks); the second and third trimester of pregnancy dataset (pregnant week: 23 to less than or equal 35 weeks). Due to the variability and irregularity of pregnancy examination dates, some samples will be lost. In this work, we deleted the samples that lacked key features. For example, a sample only has basic features such as height and weight, but it lacks all important features such as gestational sac size, FAC, HC and so on. Moreover, samples with more than 50% missing values were excluded from further analysis. The antenatal examination data is time series data and linear interpolation is suitable for missing value filling of time series data. The missing values of our data were filled by linear interpolation according to the time of two adjacent pregnancy examinations. After data preprocessing, the pregnancy dataset was obtained includes 33,222 pregnancy examination records and ultrasound records of 5537 pregnant women. Table describes the features of the dataset. Feature importance and feature selection We used GBDT to selected the features that have vital influences on EDD. The selected features were used as the input of the prediction model, which reduced the dimension of the input and solved the problem of information redundancy. Feature importance reflected the contribution of each variable in EDD. The results for feature selection of different datasets results are shown in Fig. a, c. The GSL was the most important variable to affect EDD in the first pregnancy dataset, followed by GSW, GSH, P-W, Age, MC and MD (Fig. a). At the same time, FAC was the feature with the highest weight value in the second and third trimester of pregnancy dataset, followed by FL, HC, BPD, AFI, UH, P-W, HGB, DBP, BLG, BMI, Age and SBP (Fig. c). We added the features one by one according to the weights from high to low. The corresponding MAE values and running time after training the different number of features with GBDT are shown in Fig. b, d. We chose the feature group with the shortest running time in the case of the lowest MAE. Finally, seven features were retained in the first pregnancy dataset and 13 features were reserved in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy data. Table shows the summary statistics of these parameters. Evaluation and comparison of different models In order to effectively evaluate the experimental results of GBDT-GRU model, we compared the prediction results of the Naegele’s rule and some machine learning models. The machine learning models we used for comparison include Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Regression (SVR) and LSTM. RF is a powerful algorithm for classification and regression, the prediction is made by majority vote or averaging the results of the ensemble , . SVR is an extension of the concept of Support Vector Machine (SVM), which is used for regression purpose. Based on the above-mentioned features in Table , we constructed these machine learning models to predict the EDD. The average values of the results after fivefold cross-validation are shown in Table . We provided a performance comparison of the prediction models in different datasets. First, GBDT, RF and SVR were used to predict the initial EDD from the first trimester of pregnancy dataset. Second, the final EDD was gained with the time series model based on the fused dataset. Finally, MSE, R 2 and training time were used to compare the prediction results of different models. Table shows that the GBDT-GRU prediction model outperforms Naegele’s rule, all the single models and other hybrid models, achieves average MSE of 41.73 and R 2 of 0.84. Moreover, comparing with the hybrid LSTM models, the hybrid GRU models have a shorter training time. According to the difference between EDD and the actual date of delivery, we recorded and compared the accuracy rate of each model under four categories: D bias smaller or equal to zero, two, four and six. The accuracy of different methods under different D bias is shown in Fig. . As shown in Fig. , our GBDT-GRU models achieved better prediction results than other methods for different D bias . The accuracy of EDD by GBDT-GRU model was 6.9%, 32.6%, 53.6% and 69.8%, when D bias < = 0, 2, 4 and 6 days. Significantly, with the increase of D bias , the accuracy advantage of GBDT-GRU model is more obvious. The accuracy of the GBDT-GRU model was superior to other prediction methods. In addition, we selected the features that have great influence on the EDD to make the model have better performance of prediction. The experimental results showed that the performance of hybrid models (GBDT-GRU, GBDT-LSTM, RF-GRU and RF-LSTM) were better than all single models.
